claims.text: TiVNbTa is a refractory high-entropy alloy originally designed as a single-phase solid solution.
Controlled trace oxygen and nitrogen segregate to TiVNbTa grain boundaries during thermal aging near 700°C.
Oxygen and nitrogen segregation depletes interstitial strengthening solutes from the grain interiors.
The proposed segregation and solute depletion reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes premature crack nucleation under mechanical loading.
Premature crack nucleation caused by impurity segregation leads to brittle fracture.
The initial TiVNbTa alloy is uniform and single phase, with minimal impurity levels.
Thermal aging accelerates oxygen and nitrogen segregation to grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation creates vulnerable crack-initiation sites by depleting beneficial solutes and weakening interfaces.
Higher oxygen and nitrogen impurity levels will decrease fracture toughness relative to purer TiVNbTa samples.
Higher impurity levels will shift TiVNbTa toward brittle failure modes.
The as-cast TiVNbTa baseline has a stable single-phase structure before thermal aging.
The proposed behavior applies around 700°C under service conditions where thermal-aging processes dominate.
The proposed behavior may not extend to lower-temperature service or transient thermal regimes.
Unintentional precipitate formation may also influence the aging-induced mechanical response.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is an as-cast, unaged alloy, whereas the falsification experiment ages all samples and says only impurity content is varied. This leaves it unclear whether the operative control is an unaged as-cast sample or an equally aged low-impurity sample, and comparison with the former would confound impurity content with aging.

The conditions and boundary frame the claim as elevated-temperature mechanical service around 700°C, but the experiment specifies only aging at 700°C followed by tensile testing and does not state that loading occurs at 700°C. Thus the proposed test does not unambiguously match the claimed service boundary.
